name: David and Bathsheba
charge: Adultery and the arranged death of Uriah
summary: The king took another man's wife, and when she conceived, engineered her husband's death to cover it. The prophet Nathan exposed it with a parable, and David confessed, but the consequences ran through his house for years.
offense: At the season when kings went forth to battle, David remained in Jerusalem. He saw Bathsheba, inquired after her, and was told that she was Uriah's wife before he sent messengers and took her (2 Samuel 11:1-4). Knowledge of the marriage stood before the act. The king's power to summon did not give him a right to another man's wife. When Bathsheba sent word that she was with child, David recalled Uriah from the war. Questions about Joab, the people, and the battle covered the purpose of bringing him home. Uriah would not go to his house while the ark, Israel, Judah, and his lord's servants remained in tents and the open fields (2 Samuel 11:6-11). His faithfulness frustrated the concealment. David then made him drunk, but Uriah still did not go home. The king turned from arranging an appearance to arranging a death. Uriah carried the letter ordering Joab to place him in the hottest battle and retire from him. Other servants fell with him, and David answered the report by saying that the sword devoured one as well as another (2 Samuel 11:13-25). The language of ordinary losses concealed a deliberately ordered killing. After mourning, Bathsheba became David's wife and bore a son. The matter appeared settled within the king's house, but it displeased the Lord (2 Samuel 11:26-27). Adultery had been followed by deceit and bloodshed. Deuteronomy 27:24 pronounces a curse upon the man who secretly smites his neighbour; a command carried through another man's hands did not remove David's responsibility.
judgment: Nathan brought the case of a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. David burned with anger and pronounced judgment before Nathan answered, “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:1-7). The king who could see the cruelty in a parable had concealed the same disregard in his own house. The Lord named what he had given David and what David had despised. Uriah's death was charged to David even though the sword was the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:7-9). Neither the battlefield nor Joab's obedience could stand between the king and the deed he had ordered. The sword would not depart from his house. Evil would arise within it, and his wives would be taken openly, answering what he had done secretly (2 Samuel 12:10-12). David confessed his sin without charging the people or the circumstances. Nathan declared that the Lord had put away his sin and that David would not die, yet the child would die because the deed had given occasion to the Lord's enemies to blaspheme (2 Samuel 12:13-14). Forgiveness and the removal of every consequence were not the same thing. David fasted and pleaded while the child lived. When the child died, he arose, washed, worshipped, and ate, acknowledging that he could not bring him back (2 Samuel 12:15-23). The judgment had not ceased to be the Lord's judgment because David had wept beneath it. Solomon was afterward born, and the Lord loved him (2 Samuel 12:24-25). Mercy continued in the house, but Amnon's death, Absalom's rebellion, and the taking of the concubines before Israel showed that Nathan's word had not fallen. The king was restored to life and service without being permitted to call the offense harmless.

entries.commentary: After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child. Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down. David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also. David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city. Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High. It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.

The Most High sent Nathan unto David, who told him of two men in one city, one rich and one poor. The rich man had many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing save one little ewe lamb he had bought and nourished up, which was unto him as a daughter. When a traveler came, the rich man spared his own flock and took the poor man's lamb. David's anger was greatly kindled, and he said the man that had done this shall surely die and restore the lamb fourfold, because he had no pity. Nathan came to David with a parable. When David judged that the man deserved to die for taking the poor man's one lamb, he was unknowingly pronouncing sentence on himself.

Nathan said unto David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the Most High: I anointed thee king over Israel, delivered thee out of the hand of Saul, gave thee thy master's house and wives, and the house of Israel and of Judah, and would have given thee more. Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment to do evil, killing Uriah the Hittite with the sword and taking his wife, slaying him with the sword of the children of Ammon? The Most High said if David would have just asked, He would have given him anything, for He had already given him the kingdom, Saul's house, and protection from Saul. The commandment David despised was what was read in [Deuteronomy 27](/bible/deuteronomy/27). There is a term called suicide by cop; David committed murder by the hand of another nation, because he set the whole thing up.

Thus saith the Most High: Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house, because thou hast despised me and taken the wife of Uriah to be thy wife. Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes and give them unto thy neighbour, who shall lie with them in the sight of the sun. Thou didst it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun. As the four chapters go on, and beyond, you are going to see the fruition of what just happened worked out in David's own house.

David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the Most High. Nathan said the Most High hath also put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Most High to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die. The judgment of David was that child being put to death. This goes back to Exodus 34: the Most High keeps mercy and forgives iniquity, but will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children. David got pardoned, but he did not get cleared; the punishment was still coming, one part the men of Israel dying in battle, the other his son having to die and his house having nothing but trouble.

Nathan departed, and the Most High struck the child, so that it was very sick. David besought God for the child, fasted, and lay all night upon the earth, refusing to rise or eat with the elders of his house. On the seventh day the child died, and the servants feared to tell him. When David perceived by their whispering that the child was dead, he arose, washed, anointed himself, changed his apparel, worshiped in the house of the Most High, and then ate bread. When asked why, he said that while the child lived he fasted and wept, for who could tell whether God would be gracious; but now the child was dead, he could not bring him back, he would go to him but the child would not return to him. David did all the fasting and prayer before the child died because he knew it was of the Most High that this would happen; no amount of prayer would bring the child back. David was content, saying he did not want it to happen but had no choice in the matter, for the Most High had said it would be so.

David comforted Bathsheba his wife, went in unto her, and she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon; and the Most High loved him, and sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, who called his name Jedidiah, because of the Most High. Through David's judgment, Solomon was still able to be born; it was all part of the plan of the Most High. The backup master plan behind everything was Christ, who still had to be born through David's lineage; David was still loved and still forgiven, which shows repentance, and that even the mighty among us can fall and yet rise back up.

Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon and took the royal city, then sent for David to gather the rest of the people and take the city, lest it be called after Joab's name. David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, took it, and took the king's crown of a talent of gold with the precious stones, and set it on his head. He brought forth great spoil, put the people to labor under saws and axes of iron and to the brickkiln, and did so unto all the cities of Ammon, then returned to Jerusalem. David won against the children of Ammon once again. What we gather from these four chapters is that David was called, he was king, a very mighty man, but he slipped and fell; he had godly sorrow, and in that godly sorrow he was not put to death. If he had been, there would be no Solomon, and through that no Christ. The only one perfect in this world was Christ, in whom there was no iniquity; but the men before us, when they failed, had godly sorrow, repented, and kept the commandments of the Most High even after they fell, rising back up again. --- Topics: [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

To the chief musician, a Psalm of David, written after Nathan the prophet came to him following his sin with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah one of the soldiers in David's army. Nathan got on David about it and corrected him. Now David sends up this prayer, asking the Most High for forgiveness. David appeals to the loving kindness and tender mercies of the Most High, asking that his transgressions be blotted out.
David asks to be washed thoroughly from his iniquity and cleansed from his sin. The question is: how are we going to be washed? -

David says, "I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me." That is something we must do: acknowledge our transgressions. A lot of people do not think we deserve to come over here on slave ships or deserve to be shot down in the streets or deserve the curses put on us. But we sinned against the Most High. The pants your grandma loved wearing, the auntie who thinks she can teach in the church, standing before the scriptures with a covered head, men and women with the head wrong; we set light by the Commandments as if these are small things. We sinned against the Most High. -

Against the Most High only has David sinned and done this evil in his sight, that the Most High might be justified when he speaks and clear when he judges. We are not going to stand before the Most High and be justified talking about "me and Jesus." If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God. Wearing pants, not wearing fringes, crossdressing; none of that will be excused. -
David was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did his mother conceive him, meaning he was born from a natural childbirth.
The Most High desires truth in the inward parts, and in the hidden part he makes us to know wisdom.

Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean; wash me and I shall be whiter than snow. David says this for a reason, because the ordinances set up in the earth are patterned after what goes on in the heavens, and Christ is our high priest. -
Make me to hear joy and gladness, that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice. This does not mean the Most High literally broke his bones; it means correction. -
Hide thy face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. Blessed is the man whose transgressions are covered.
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. We must understand what we read; this is a renewing of the mind, like Nicodemus asking how a man can be born again. -
Cast me not away from thy presence, and take not thy holy spirit from me. The best thing going for us is to be in the presence of the Most High. -

Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation and uphold me with thy free spirit. David understood the importance of losing the kingdom; from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom suffers violence, and they kill us and get away with it. That is the wages of sin. -
Then will I teach transgressors thy ways, and sinners shall be converted unto thee.
Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, because David had killed the man. The true baptism is not the dipping in water but the answer of a good conscience toward the Most High. -
O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall show forth thy praise.
For thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it; thou delightest not in burnt offerings. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David. -
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken and a contrite heart, which the Most High will not despise. Contrite means meek and teachable. -
Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion; build thou the walls of Jerusalem. In captivity we are like those who built the wall with one hand and fought with the other; it is time to rebuild a nation.
Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering; then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.

Abijam reigns three years in Jerusalem and walks in all the sins of his father, his heart not perfect with the Most High as David's was. The children did what they saw their fathers do, not merely what was said, which is why the Most High teaches His people to be different. Yet for David's sake the Most High gives him a lamp in Jerusalem, because David did right all his days save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, a wrong from which David repented. -

After Abijam dies, Asa his son reigns forty-one years and does right in the eyes of the Most High as David his father did. Asa takes the sodomites out of the land, removes the idols his fathers made, and even removes his own mother Maachah from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, which he destroys and burns at the brook Kidron. Though the high places are not removed, Asa's heart is perfect with the Most High all his days, and he brings dedicated silver, gold, and vessels into the house of the Most High.

There is war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel, who builds Ramah to cut off passage to and from Asa. Asa takes silver and gold from the house of the Most High and the king's house and sends it to Benhadad of Syria to break his league with Baasha, and Benhadad smites cities of Israel so Baasha stops building Ramah. Asa uses the stones and timber of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. In his old age he is diseased in his feet, then sleeps with his fathers, and Jehoshaphat his son reigns in his place.

Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel two years and does evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha conspires against him, kills him, and reigns in his place, then smites all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite. This fulfills, years later, the judgment that Jeroboam's descendants would be destroyed for the sins by which he made Israel to sin.

Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah and does evil, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin by which he made Israel to sin. The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming.

verses.text: And it came to pass in an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed, and walked upon the roof of the king’s house: and from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.
And David sent and enquired after the woman. And one said, Is not this Bath–sheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?
And David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in unto him, and he lay with her; for she was purified from her uncleanness: and she returned unto her house.
And it came to pass in the morning, that David wrote a letter to Joab, and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
And he wrote in the letter, saying, Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.
And it came to pass, when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were.
And the men of the city went out, and fought with Joab: and there fell some of the people of the servants of David; and Uriah the Hittite died also.
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;

And I gave thee thy master’s house, and thy master’s wives into thy bosom, and gave thee the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that had been too little, I would moreover have given unto thee such and such things.

Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment of the Lord, to do evil in his sight? thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and hast taken his wife to be thy wife, and hast slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon.
Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house; because thou hast despised me, and hast taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be thy wife.

Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun.
For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.
And David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the Lord. And Nathan said unto David, The Lord also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.
Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die.
Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.
For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
Because David did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, and turned not aside from any thing that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.
